articles.title: US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough, Zelensky tells BBC
articles.summary: Ukraine's president voices frustration with US and says it is "strange" Trump has described Vladimir Putin as a friend.
articles.preview: Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and complaining that the US is not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks. In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president also said it was "strange" that Donald Trump had posted a photo of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as "my friend". "Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
articles.body:
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and complaining that the US is not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks.

In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president also said it was "strange" that Donald Trump had posted a photo of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as "my friend".

"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.

"He's an aggressor, and a killerâ¦He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.

Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.

Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.

The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

He said talks were expected to resume in December.

On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".

But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions â on everything.

And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.

The Kremlin appears to be resisting.

- Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say

- Published7 days ago

- Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend

- Published5 days ago

Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.

Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.

So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".

"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.

The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.

In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.

Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.

Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.

But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Amercians were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.

"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them moreâ¦ It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.

"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."

He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink â and its military version, Starshield â were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.

Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.

So whose decision was that?

"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."

Tough winter

Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.

On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.

Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".

He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.

He declined to be more specific.

But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.

Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.

Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.

They have also plunged much of the city into darkness.

"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.

"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

articles.title: With eyes on Malaysia’s next federal election, major coalitions steer clear of Sarawak polls
articles.summary: Experts say that Malaysia's major political coalitions are reluctant to antagonise Gabungan Parti Sarawak, whose support could prove crucial in forming the next federal government.
articles.preview: analysis Asia Experts say that Malaysia's major political coalitions are reluctant to antagonise Gabungan Parti Sarawak, whose support could prove crucial in forming the next federal government. KUALA LUMPUR: Sarawak’s 13th state polls next month is shaping up to be relatively subdued, not because the stakes are low, analysts say but because major political coalitions based in West Malaysia are sitting it out in order to stay on Gabungan Parti Sarawak’s (GPS) good side ahead of the next federal election.
articles.body:
analysis Asia

Experts say that Malaysia's major political coalitions are reluctant to antagonise Gabungan Parti Sarawak, whose support could prove crucial in forming the next federal government.

KUALA LUMPUR: Sarawak’s 13th state polls next month is shaping up to be relatively subdued, not because the stakes are low, analysts say but because major political coalitions based in West Malaysia are sitting it out in order to stay on Gabungan Parti Sarawak’s (GPS) good side ahead of the next federal election.

GPS - the incumbent government - has announced that it will contest all 82 seats in the Dec 12 polls. But ahead of nomination day on Saturday (Nov 28), component parties within the Barisan Nasional (BN) and Perikatan Nasional (PN) coalitions have said they will not contest the election.

Within Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s ruling Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition, Parti Keadilan Rakyat (PKR) and Parti Amanah Negara (Amanah) have also opted out.

Meanwhile, the Democratic Action Party (DAP) - a PH component - has so far announced 12 candidates for the upcoming polls, alongside an electoral pact with local party Parti Bansa Dayak Sarawak (PBDS).

Political analyst Syahruddin Awang Ahmad from the Universiti Malaysia Sabah (UMS) told CNA that the polls represent a “strategic ceasefire” that is driven equally by electoral pragmatism and federal power preservation.

The Sarawak state election is the fourth one to be held this year - after earlier polls in Johor, Negeri Sembilan and Melaka.

Related:

“Malaysia’s fractured federal landscape transforms GPS’ parliamentary seats into indispensable kingmakers ahead of the 16th General Election (GE16), due by early 2028. Neither the unity government nor PN dares provoke premier Abang Johari,” he said, in reference to GPS chairman and caretaker Sarawak premier Abang Johari Openg.

“Consequently, this subdued contest is a calculated retreat where they want to avoid humiliating deposit losses while banking political capital with GPS for post-GE16 coalition negotiations.”

During the 2021 Sarawak state election, 169 out of 349 candidates lost their RM5,000 (US$1,200) election deposits for failing to secure at least one-eighth of the total votes cast.

This included 22 out of 28 PKR candidates, all eight Amanah candidates, three out of 26 DAP candidates, and 23 out of 70 candidates from Parti Sarawak Bersatu (PSB). PSB had been GPS’ biggest challenger in 2021, winning four seats and finishing second overall in the popular vote before dissolving to merge with a GPS component party.

WHY COALITIONS ARE STEPPING BACK

For most observers and political parties, a sweeping GPS victory is already a foregone conclusion. Prior to the dissolution of the assembly last month, GPS had held a supermajority - or more than two-thirds of seats - in the state parliament.

James Chin, a professor of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania told CNA that GPS has a stranglehold of the constituencies in the state, with only a handful of urban Chinese-majority seats seen as genuinely competitive.

“This number is nowhere near enough to form a state government. The reason why it’s a quiet election is because everybody expects GPS to win without much problem. This is just based on simple maths. I always say that it is more of a popularity poll than an electoral poll,” he said.

GPS was formed in June 2018 and contested its maiden state election in 2021 under its own banner, sweeping 76 of the 82 seats. PSB’s dissolution in 2024 and merger with one of GPS’ component parties allowed the coalition to increase its seats to 79. One former PSB assemblyman chose to become an independent.

The remaining two seats prior to the dissolution of the state legislative assembly belonged to DAP.

Before the 2021 state election, BN had always held at least a two-thirds majority in the Sarawak state assembly.

GPS’ four component parties - Parti Pesaka Bumiputera Bersatu (PBB), Parti Rakyat Sarawak (PRS), Progressive Democratic Party (PDP) and Sarawak United People’s Party (SUPP) - had previously been part of BN.

But it left the coalition to form GPS after BN lost power at the federal level for the first time in the 2018 general election on the back of the multibillion-dollar 1MDB corruption scandal.

Jayum Jawan of the Institute of Borneo Studies in Universiti Malaysia Sarawak added that Peninsular Malaysia’s-style of politics has struggled to gain traction in Sarawak, pointing out that the United Malaysia National Organsation (UMNO) - a BN lynchpin party - was never allowed to set up in the state.

“That brand of Malay-Muslim dominance politics promoted in the peninsula simply won’t work in Sarawak. No leaders are going to welcome such politics openly because they don’t want to offend the Dayak and Chinese communities,” he said.

But beyond the anticipated outcome on Dec 12, analysts say the subdued contest is tied directly to federal political survival ahead of GE16. Anwar had said on Nov 25 that the federal election will likely take place before or after the country’s National Day in August next year.

Sarawak’s 31 parliamentary seats - 23 of which are held by GPS - make the coalition courted by all political coalitions based in Peninsular Malaysia.

Chin said that to form the federal government, any coalition will ultimately need the support of GPS and Gabungan Rakyat Sabah (GRS).

“This explains why UMNO/BN and PAS are currently playing nice with GPS by choosing not to contest. It is a calculated move to ease coalition negotiations after GE16,” he said, referring to the PN component party Parti Islam Se-Malaysia.

BN chairman and Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said on Nov 15 that the coalition would not contest any seats in the Sarawak state election, in line with a longstanding understanding between UMNO and PBB.

Meanwhile, PAS announced on Nov 19 that it would also sit out the polls after taking into account current political developments and other considerations, saying it remained committed to strengthening unity and political stability.

This was the first time since 1996 that PAS would not contest the polls, although it had never won a seat in the state before.

Fellow PN component party - Parti Wawasan Malaysia - also said it would not contest the polls, and would instead support the campaigns of local parties.

Still, Jayum cautioned that no one should take GPS’ loyalty for granted simply by avoiding a clash on its home turf, saying that the Sarawak-based coalition would throw its weight behind whichever coalition emerges strongest after a federal poll.

“GPS will support any coalition that appears to lead and has a legitimate claim to form the government. No coalition will attack them so much because of their potential support later on,” he said.

On Nov 22, Abang Johari questioned why political partners at the federal level wanted to contest against them in the Sarawak polls.

“The federal government is not there without GPS’ support. Why should loyal friends contest against each other?,” he said, adding that they were, however, ready to fight anyone who wanted to contest.

Then, on Nov 25, Anwar’s PKR announced that it would not contest in the state polls, citing the need to preserve political stability and cooperation with GPS within the federal unity government.

The decision came a day after Home Minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail, who is also PKR deputy president and PH secretary-general, visited Abang Johari in Kuching.

PKR contested 28 seats in the 2021 state election, failing to win any of them.

Syahruddin said that PKR’s complete withdrawal removes any party-specific incentive for Anwar to stump on the ground and that campaigning openly for DAP against GPS would trigger an existential crisis within his own unity government.

“Anwar has repeatedly cautioned coalition allies against airing disagreements publicly, knowing that antagonising Abang Johari could unravel the parliamentary stability keeping him in office ahead of GE16,” he said.

WHERE THE ELECTORAL FIGHTS WILL TAKE PLACE

PKR’s decision, however, has not gone down well with DAP which announced that it will contest 12 seats, less than half the 26 seats it fought in 2021.

Sarawak DAP chairman Chong Chieng Jen in a Facebook video on Nov 25 criticised PKR’s decision to sit out the polls as "sacrificing democracy in Sarawak" for political support at the federal level.

He claimed that Anwar had caved in to the threat by the demands of GPS to sit out the election.

“We strongly believe that Sarawak will be better if there is a stronger opposition to keep the ruling party in check. Check and balance is the cornerstone to good governance.

"Elections must not be seen as a destabilising force in any democratic society … Otherwise there is no need for any election,” said Chong, who will be contesting the Kota Sentosa seat.

Syahruddin said that Sarawak DAP has abandoned regime-change rhetoric entirely and was campaigning strictly as a constructive urban watchdog, asking Chinese-majority constituencies to elect local checks and balances to scrutinise state spending.

But Chin said that DAP faces an uphill battle, noting that Abang Johari has avoided racial politics and rolled out popular policies - such as free tertiary education in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) - that have resonated with Chinese voters.

Jayum said that the only pockets of genuine electoral excitement lie in Chinese-majority seats and a handful of Dayak constituencies - the non-Muslim indigenous communities of the state - though GPS is still expected to retain a comfortable margin overall.

He noted that while PBDS - which has an electoral pact with DAP - has unveiled 26 candidates and tapped into the grievances among rural Dayak voters, the revived party lacks seasoned heavyweights capable of unseating GPS incumbents.

“I don’t believe that one party should win a supermajority, because there is always a need for checks and balances but some are saying that GPS could even win every seat this time around,” said Jayum.

articles.title: Two Italians killed in strike in Kuwait, as Iran denies responsibility
articles.summary: The pair were technicians for German company Rheinmetall, according to Italy's foreign ministry.
articles.preview: Two Italian nationals have died following a strike on a facility in Kuwait which both countries have blamed on Iran. The pair were technicians working for German arms manufacturing company Rheinmetall, Italy's foreign ministry said. Iran has denied responsibility for the attack, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying the incident looked "suspicious" and that Tehran would work with Kuwait and Italy to "determine the cause".
articles.body:
Two Italian nationals have died following a strike on a facility in Kuwait which both countries have blamed on Iran.

The pair were technicians working for German arms manufacturing company Rheinmetall, Italy's foreign ministry said.

Iran has denied responsibility for the attack, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying the incident looked "suspicious" and that Tehran would work with Kuwait and Italy to "determine the cause".

Kuwait's defence ministry said earlier that four people - the two Italians, a Kuwaiti national and Pakistani national - had been injured from falling shrapnel after a number of drones from Iran were detected and intercepted.

It comes just over a week after Kuwait said it had repelled overnight Iranian drone attacks on an airbase which hosts US forces - the first strikes in more than two months on the country.

Recent exchanges of fire between the US and Iran, and a deadlock in negotiations, have raised fears of a major escalation in the war.

The conflict began when US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, with Iran retaliating by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.

On Thursday, Araghchi said he had expressed condolences over the deaths in calls with his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts and that the incident looked like a "precooked recipe for war", without expanding further.

Earlier, the country's armed forces spokesperson Abolfazl Shekarchi said "no military or offensive operations have been conducted" by Iran.

Kuwait's Army said the latest attack was on a "vital site in the country" and was the result of "heinous Iranian aggression", while confirming the deaths of the two Italian nationals.

Italy's foreign minister was quoted by Italian media as saying that investigations showed that the drone used in the attack was manufactured in Iran and that Iranian proxies were known to carry out attacks in the region.

"The Rheinmetall Group is in deep mourning," the German firm said in a statement confirming the deaths of two of its staff members.

"Two highly valued employees lost their lives while carrying out their professional duties, as they were providing technical support for air defence systems," it added.

"Protecting people in the country was a matter of profound importance to them.

"Company management and the workforce are devastated that our colleagues have now lost their lives."

Italian media outlets have named the two individuals. One of the men was reported to be 36, while the other was 65 and nearing retirement.

The men had been performing maintenance on systems used by the Kuwait Armed Forces, according to Italian press agency Ansa citing Italy's foreign ministry.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on X: "On my own behalf and on behalf of the government, I express my deepest sympathy and offer my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families.

"My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families."

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on social media: "We must step up pressure on Iran to end these unacceptable attacks against its neighbours and our partners in the Gulf.

"Today's events are a further reminder that security in the Gulf is a security issue for us all."

articles.title: Albania's youth are protesting in Flamingo Revolution, not leaving the country anymore
articles.summary: Youth protests against a rigid political system and corruption have shaken the government of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama. They also show that fewer young people are willing to emigrate in search of a better future.
articles.preview: Albania's youth are protesting, not leaving the country anymore November 26, 2026 Youth protests against a rigid political system and corruption have shaken the government of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama. They also show that fewer young people are willing to emigrate in search of a better future. In mid-October, students in the Albanian capital Tirana set a suitcase on fire and threw it into the courtyard of the Education Ministry.
articles.body:
Albania's youth are protesting, not leaving the country anymore

November 26, 2026

Youth protests against a rigid political system and corruption have shaken the government of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama. They also show that fewer young people are willing to emigrate in search of a better future.

In mid-October, students in the Albanian capital Tirana set a suitcase on fire and threw it into the courtyard of the Education Ministry. Everyone in the country understood the symbolism: According to the 2023 census, the population of this Western Balkan country shrunk by about 420,000 between 2011 and 2023 — by nearly 15% — primarily because of emigration.

For a generation of young Albanians, this was the response to a system that gave them little voice. But now young people want to stay, and the protesters are saying that the system has to change.

Known as the "Flamingo Revolution," the social movement began in May with demonstrations against a luxury resort in a coastal reserve that US President Donald Trump's daughter Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner were involved in.

It quickly evolved into broader criticism against corruption, Prime Minister Edi Rama's government and his ruling Socialist Party and the country's entire political class.

Thousands marched almost every evening for four months in protests that were largely peaceful. But on October 13, a student protest escalated and there were clashes with police. Since then, the unrest has continued, with police using tear gas, water cannons and rubber bullets against demonstrators. There have been hundreds of arrests and many injuries, amid damage to public and private property.

'Flamingo revolution' has broad support

The protesters have called for Rama's resignation, a transitional government, electoral reform and fresh elections. The movement, which has no leader, has support from people across the political spectrum. And while the prime minister has blamed "foreign hands" for the movement, there seems to be little evidence that external actors are orchestrating the protests, though they may have attempted to exploit the unrest online.

The protesters, who do not feel represented by Albania's democracy, are driven by domestic issues: corruption, the high cost of living and low wages. This is nothing new, but many factors have converged recently: a series of high-level corruption charges, including against ministers and two of Rama's former deputies, rising prices and the fact that Albania is being measured against EU standards by a new generation.

In certain areas, Rama has transformed Albania since taking office in 2013: the economy has grown significantly, as the government likes to point out, and tourism is booming. But the prosperity remains unevenly distributed. Critics accuse the government of channeling too much taxpayer money into a small number of well-connected companies through prestigious projects and public-private partnerships, and in some cases through corrupt business deals, at the expense of healthcare, education and better economic prospects for the wider population.

Rama has rejected the calls for his resignation and has invited protesters to engage in dialogue, which they have so far refused.

Alternating between Socialist and Democratic Party

In 2008, Rama and Sali Berisha, the long-time chairman of the opposition Democratic Party, worked on a reform to Albania's constitution and electoral law, which was approved by parliament. Since then, it is party leaders who have determined who enters Parliament, which weakens ties between lawmakers and their constituents.

In addition, it has become significantly more difficult for new parties to win seats. In 2025, a new party received about 64,000 votes, but only one seat. The Socialists, by contrast, won about one seat for every 10,000 votes.

Rama has been the leader of the Socialists since 2005, while Berisha first became the chairman of the Democratic Party in 1991. For 21 years, Albania's prime minister has either been Rama or Berisha. Freedom House, a US nongovernmental organization that promotes democracy worldwide, classifies Albania as "partly free" and describes the country's political parties as being "often organized around leading personalities."

Protesters on the streets have said that they want both men to be jailed. Rama has argued that governments should be replaced at the ballot box, not on the streets.

Though the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) acknowledged that parliamentary elections in 2025 were "competitive and professionally managed" it said that they had taken place "in a highly polarized environment and contestants did not enjoy a level playing field."

It added that there were "reports of intimidation, misuse of public resources and pressure on public employees, which undermined equal opportunities."

The Democratic Party also spoke of election fraud and intimidation. Turnout was below 45%.

Protesters call out corruption, face high cost of living

Many protesters also allege that when it comes to business, what matters is the proximity to people in power. They criticize the public procurement, public auctions and concessions system, which has led to state-owned land, including coastal and protected areas, being sold to private investors.

Ordinary Albanians are feeling the financial brunt. According to the Albanian Institute of Statistics (INSTAT), half of all employees earn less than 60,000 lek (roughly €620 or $680) per month after taxes. But according to Eurostat, food prices are slightly above the EU average and real estate prices in Tirana have nearly doubled since 2018, with rents rising just as quickly.

For many years, young Albanians who were dissatisfied with the system opted to leave the country. The number of Albanian citizens in Germany more than doubled between 2018 and 2024, reaching almost 120,000.

Though it is still too early to say whether there are fewer Albanians leaving today, for many protesters staying has become a political statement.

Albanians largely pro-EU

Rama has argued that his resignation would jeopardize Albania's bid to join the European Union by 2030, but the vast majority of Albanians are pro-European, including those on the streets and in the opposition. From the protesters' perspective, it is the government headed by Rama that is the real obstacle on the path to the EU.

Though there is currently a wave of protests across Europe, the only obvious comparison is with Serbia, where a student-led movement recently forced a long-time ruler from office. Whether Albania will follow this example depends on whether young people, who have traditionally not been deeply engaged in politics, can turn their protests into votes.

What is certain is that for three decades, Albania's leaders have relied on their citizens' suitcases. Now, the country's students have burned that very luggage.

Andi Balla is a doctoral candidate at the Leibniz Institute for East and Southeast European Studies (IOS) in Regensburg, where he is conducting research on demographic debates in Albania. He has written numerous articles on Albania for an international audience.

This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Belgium: Farmers and tractors descend on Brussels to defend EU subsidies
articles.summary: Around 200 representatives of European farming unions marched through Brussels, Belgium, on Thursday 26 November 2026 to protest against proposed cuts to the European Union's Common Agricultural Policy (CAP). The demonstration coincided with a summit on the bloc's next long-term budget.
articles.preview: Around 200 representatives of European farming unions marched through Brussels, Belgium, on Thursday 26 November 2026 to protest against proposed cuts to the European Union's Common Agricultural Policy (CAP). The demonstration coincided with a summit on the bloc's next long-term budget.
articles.body: Rolling into Brussels’ European quarter alongside a convoy of tractors, protesters marched past the European Parliament with banners demanding that agricultural funding be protected, one machine bearing a stark placard reading "Agriculture for sale, €0". Chanting slogans against looming cuts, demonstrators echoed warnings from farming unions that subsidies could drop by 20% under the EU’s next long-term budget, tightening the squeeze on already strained rural incomes — a plight underscored by Lucas Bierlaire of the Walloon Farmers Federation, who warned that many growers were already struggling to make a decent living. The rally coincided with a two-day summit in which EU leaders are locked in fractious talks over the bloc’s 2028-2034 budget, divided over the European Commission’s proposed €2 trillion spending plan that would substantially erode agricultural support in real terms. Arnaud Rousseau, head of France’s largest farming union, the FNSEA, urged Brussels to show greater ambition for European agriculture despite fiscal pressures, ahead of a follow-up summit in mid-December aimed at sealing a deal before the year’s end.

articles.title: US-backed Ebola quarantine centre violated constitution, Kenyan court rules
articles.summary: A Kenyan court on Thursday ruled that the government had breached the constitution by allowing the construction of a US-backed Ebola quarantine site at a military base in Laikipia.
articles.preview: Kenya Kenya’s government violated the Constitution by allowing the construction of a US-backed Ebola quarantine facility without public participation, a senior court ruled on Thursday. The 50-bed facility at a military base in Laikipia sparked deadly protests by residents who feared exposure to the virus and an outbreak that could overwhelm Kenya's fragile health system.
articles.body:
Kenya

Kenya’s government violated the Constitution by allowing the construction of a US-backed Ebola quarantine facility without public participation, a senior court ruled on Thursday.

The 50-bed facility at a military base in Laikipia sparked deadly protests by residents who feared exposure to the virus and an outbreak that could overwhelm Kenya's fragile health system.

In May, the High Court had ordered construction of the facility to be halted pending the determination of a case filed by the Law Society of Kenya and constitutional watchdog Katiba Institute. The petitioners argued that Kenya’s fragile health system was ill-equipped to handle a potential Ebola outbreak.

Trump administration officials had said Americans exposed to Ebola abroad would be sent to the facility rather than flown home. The US government planned to commit $13.5 million to Kenya’s Ebola preparedness efforts.

Justice Patricia Nyaundi on Thursday ordered the government to disclose all agreements with the US within 45 days. She also barred further construction or operations at the facility.

Residents reported seeing military aircraft landing at the base shortly after construction began. A US-based humanitarian group also said some of its staff members who had been working in Congo had been quarantined in Kenya.

Kenya reported its first-ever Ebola case in October, after a Kenyan national traveled from Congo through Uganda. The country recorded a total of nine cases, all involving direct contacts of the initial patient.

Asked in October whether the US-backed facility would also quarantine Kenyans exposed to Ebola, Health Minister Aden Duale said the government was awaiting the court’s directions.

articles.title: Protests in Iraqi Kurdistan at plans for government in Baghdad to take over oil, border crossings
articles.summary: Thousands have gathered in the capital of northern Iraq's semiautonomous Kurdish region, waving flags and voicing opposition to plans for the federal government to take control of oil operations and border crossings.
articles.preview: Mass protests in Kurdish Irbil against Iraqi government reform plans November 26, 2026 Thousands have gathered in the capital of northern Iraq's semiautonomous Kurdish region, waving flags and voicing opposition to plans for the federal government to take control of oil operations and border crossings. Protesters took to the streets of Irbil, also often written Erbil, in Iraqi Kurdistan early on Thursday in large numbers, waving massive flags of the semiautonomous region in northern Iraq.
articles.body:
Mass protests in Kurdish Irbil against Iraqi government reform plans

November 26, 2026

Thousands have gathered in the capital of northern Iraq's semiautonomous Kurdish region, waving flags and voicing opposition to plans for the federal government to take control of oil operations and border crossings.

Protesters took to the streets of Irbil, also often written Erbil, in Iraqi Kurdistan early on Thursday in large numbers, waving massive flags of the semiautonomous region in northern Iraq.

They were responding to federal government plans announced earlier in the week for Baghdad to take control of oil operations and border crossings previously run by Kurdish authorities.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi had said the measures were part of a bid to stop oil smuggling when announcing the changes.

According to state media reports, later on Thursday, Iraqi border forces closed two border crossings with Syria and Iran that had been administered by the Kurdish authorities.

Iraq's border forces commander told the Iraqi News Agency that the al-Waleed border crossing with Syria and the Bashta border crossing with Iran have been closed.

Rival Kurdish factions unite to protest plans

The plans marked an escalation in the long-running power struggle between the central government and Kurdish authorities that have largely governed themselves since 1991, albeit with varying levels of recognition and authority.

Rival Kurdish parties joined forces for the large protests in the regional capital.

Protests were also reported to have spread to several other towns and cities beyond the capital.

Iraq's 2005 constitution, written following the US-led invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein, formally recognized the Kurdish region and its government. But authorities in Erbil and Baghdad have remained in a tug of war over the control of land, oil and money ever since.

Tuesday's decision, which received backing from Iraq's Federal Supreme Court a day later, brings border crossing in the Kurdish region under federal government management. It places approval for oil exports from the region under the authority of the federal oil ministry and transfers the management of oil fields in four contested provinces — Kirkuk, Diyala, Salahuddin and Nineveh.

The Kurdish regional government's Cabinet said on Wednesday that the decision from Baghdad "violates both the Constitution and the constitutional rights of the Kurdistan region," saying it represented "an attempt to return Iraq to a centralized regime."

Prime Minister al-Zaidi, who took office earlier this year with the backing of US President Donald Trump, also dismissed Kirkuk's operations commander and police chief and the head of the Border Ports Commission. He said the measures reflected Iraq's "independent national will."

Regional Prime Minister Masrour Barzani said his government was "surprised" by al-Zaidi's decisions and called them "completely unacceptable."

Contested region even since 2005 reformation

Iraq's Supreme Court ruled on Wednesday that the authority of the Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) only covered the land it administered on March 19, 2003, the day before the US-led invasion that unseated Saddam Hussein.

Kurdish peshmerga forces moved into many disputed areas after 2003, including the oil fields covered by this week's orders.

The 2005 constitution tried to solve the fate of some of the disputed territories in the lands between the borders to Syria and Iran that are home to a host of ethnicities and communities but with Kurds generally the majority group.

Article 140 called for reversing Saddam-era policies of expelling Kurds and moving Arabs in, and called for a census and a referendum on whether the disputed regions should join the Kurdistan region. Neither was held.

Kurdish forces then gained more of the disputed territory after Iraqi forces were forced out by the so-called "Islamic State," with Kurdish pershmerga for subsequently reclaiming some of the land with some international assistance.

The oil-rich region is highly important to both administrations, in a country that relies on oil revenues for the vast majority of its public sector budget.

Internal political tensions within Iraqi Kurdistan have further complicated the issue in recent months, with the Federal Supreme Court hearing an ongoing challenge against the current government's legitimacy after a party withdrew from the coalition cabinet. But rival Kurdish political factions seem to have found common ground on this issue at least.

Nathan Fielder indaga clinicamente le idee sbagliate e le illusioni altrui, il che lo rende perfetto per Elizabeth Holmes, fondatrice della Theranos, startup della Silicon valley che pretendeva di rivoluzionare le analisi del sangue, condannata per frode a più di undici anni di carcere. È stranamente, poeticamente bello e commovente.

Richard Brody,The New Yorker

Francia 2026, 139’. In sala

Il decimo film del regista iraniano, ispirato a Breve storia d’amore di Krzysztof Kieślowski è un film interamente francese per il cast, la lingua e le ambientazioni. Sylvie (Huppert), scrittrice misantropa, per comporre la sua opera s’ispira a quello che accade nell’appartamento di fronte al suo. Con un certo virtuosismo Farhadi orchestra un complesso gioco di apparenze, perdendosi però per strada. In questo ritratto d’artista impostore finiamo per intravedere quello di un regista spinto, anche per ciò che accade nel suo paese, dall’urgenza di ridefinirsi.

Jacques Mandelbaum, Le Monde

Stati Uniti 2026, 195’. In sala

Le nuove disavventure di Cliff Booth unisce la regia meticolosa di David Fincher e la narrazione irriverente di Quentin Tarantino, dando vita a un sequel accattivante e sgangherato di C’era una volta a… Hollywood. I punti di forza di Fincher e di Tarantino sono evidenti in una pellicola la cui riuscita è dovuta soprattutto a Brad Pitt, che riprende con fascino e pathos il ruolo che lo portò all’Oscar. Nell’estate del 1977, Cliff si arrangia come può in una Los Angeles che sta diventando irriconoscibile. Tutto cambia quando incontra Karen (Debicki), agente di una star televisiva megalomane.

Tim Grierson, Screen International

Stati Uniti / Germania 2026, 104’. In sala

Un gruppo di medici volontari in alcuni villaggi lungo il rio delle Amazzoni viene a conoscenza della leggenda di Boiúna poco prima che una violenta faida tra loschi personaggi risvegli il gigantesco serpente della giungla. Nonostante il contesto e alcune evidenti attinenze, questo survival horror non è un reboot di Anaconda ed è sicuramente superiore agli altri tentativi di sfruttarne il successo.

Megan Navarro, BloodyDisgusting

Repubblica Ceca / Slovacchia 2024, 131’. In sala

Alla vigilia della primavera di Praga, il giovane Tomáš ottiene un lavoro alla radio nazionale cecoslovacca, dove i giornalisti sfidano la censura di stato. Si ritrova nel cuore di un magnifico momento di resistenza giornalistica. Questo dramma politico non è rivoluzionario nella sua forma, cioè quella di una buona e solida ricostruzione, ma intreccia eventi personali e storici con una tale tensione che si comincia a sperare in un finale diverso da quello di una primavera repressa con la forza.

Guillemette Odicino, Télérama

Spagna 2025, 107’. In sala

Gemma Blasco affronta il tema dei traumi delle donne sopravvissute alla violenza con notevole sensibilità e moderazione. Sceglie di esplorare le conseguenze dello stupro subìto dalla protagonista attraverso una narrazione non lineare che riflette il suo disorientamento, la sua solitudine e il suo tormento emotivo. Ne risulta un film profondamente introspettivo che non solo mette a nudo il carico personale del trauma, ma s’interroga anche su come gli altri reagiscono a esso, in particolare su come il dolore della vittima possa essere sfruttato da coloro che le offrono aiuto.

Mario Hernández, mundoCine

articles.title: Africa's opposition voices face growing pressure
articles.summary: Opposition politicians and government critics say arrests, prosecutions and restrictions on public activity are making it harder to challenge those in power. Is a broader pattern emerging?
articles.preview: November 26, 2026 Opposition politicians and government critics say arrests, prosecutions and restrictions on public activity are making it harder to challenge those in power. Is a broader pattern emerging? From Cameroon and Tanzania to Mozambique, Nigeria and Zambia, opposition leaders have accused authorities of limiting political freedoms through legal action and restrictions on public activity. In each case, officials have said the measures are justified under national laws and security provisions.
articles.body:
November 26, 2026

Opposition politicians and government critics say arrests, prosecutions and restrictions on public activity are making it harder to challenge those in power. Is a broader pattern emerging?

From Cameroon and Tanzania to Mozambique, Nigeria and Zambia, opposition leaders have accused authorities of limiting political freedoms through legal action and restrictions on public activity.

In each case, officials have said the measures are justified under national laws and security provisions.

"Cameroon is very sensitive, and it is important that we know when to criticize the government and when not to criticize the government openly," said Ngam Glory Ani Mbom, a citizen of the central African country.

She said fear of arrest and violence discourage political participation. "You cannot talk about democracy when opposition supporters cannot freely express their minds to the public," she told DW.

For Ndah Grimbald, deputy secretary-general of Cameroon's opposition Social Democratic Front, one of the biggest obstacles is organizing public meetings.

"The first major challenge we face as members of the opposition is the non-authorization of public rallies, public meetings," he said, noting that opposition proposals receive little attention in parliament. "Private members' bills are not even listened to."

Cameroonian law guarantees freedom of assembly but allows authorities to restrict gatherings on grounds of public order or national security. Organizers are also required to notify officials in advance.

Tanzania: Trial and prison

In Tanzania, opposition leader Tundu Lissu was arrested in April 2025 and charged with treason. In November 2026, the High Court acquitted Lissu of treason but convicted him of incitement and sentenced him to four years in prison.

Prosecutors argued that Lissu's remarks were intended to disrupt Tanzania's 2025 general election. In its ruling, the court said it was satisfied that his statements were intended to "disrupt elections and instigate violence."

Lissu rejected the verdict, calling the case "political persecution." He told the judges: "I was not charged with incitement but you judges are convicting me with it just to impress the person who gives you the titles." He added: "Excuses were created to imprison me."

Gerson Msigwa, Tanzania's chief government spokesperson, directly rejected allegations of political repression and human rights violations.

"Concerns of diminishing civic space and restrictions on political parties to engage in political processes in the lead-up to the general election are unfounded and misleading," Msigwa said in response to Amnesty International's accusations of a "wave of terror" sweeping Tanzania ahead of the 2025 vote.

Mozambique: Charges disputed

In Mozambique, opposition figure Venancio Mondlane faces five charges linked to protests after the disputed 2024 election, including incitement to terrorism and public advocacy of crime. Prosecutors have accused him of encouraging violence and civil disobedience. Mondlane has denied the allegations.

"I have more than enough evidence. There's plenty to go around. Many of my statements were precisely in the opposite direction," he told DW, adding that the protests were intended to prevent violence.

Pedro Sinai Nhatitima, a judge counselor and spokesperson for Mozambique's Supreme Court, defended the court's decision not to allow live broadcasts of Mondlane's trial. He denied that the proceedings are politically influenced, saying the court will decide the case according to the law.

Nigeria: Policing dissent?

In Nigeria, police in Borno State recently arrested five men wearing T-shirts bearing the slogan "Tinubu Must Go!"

The police said the men were not arrested for their political views, but were found with suspected drugs and other items. The men face allegations including public disturbance and thuggery.

In Kano, police blocked access to a venue for a planned meeting, citing public safety concerns.

Zambia: Courts and controversy

In Zambia, opposition leader Brian Mundubile has criticized what he describes as a retreat from democratic rights. The courts were closed on August 24, the final day for filing a presidential election petition. The judiciary cited security reasons, while police said intelligence-led security assessments were underway at several government institutions.

State House presidential aide Clayson Hamasaka denied that President Hakainde Hichilema had ordered the closure to prevent an election challenge.

The same month, former opposition lawmaker and cabinet minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was shot dead during a security operation at Mundubile's residence. Authorities said the operation followed intelligence about individuals considered a national security threat, and that officers came under gunfire and returned fire.

Mundubile, who faces treason and sedition charges with other opposition figures, has called for fairness in the proceedings. "We expect an open court process. We are innocent of all the charges against us," he said.

Zambian constitutional lawyer Linda Kasonde has warned: "As you can see, our public institutions are on trial. Democracy in Zambia is on trial."

Cameroonian political analyst Kinang Derick Fai said that despite the setbacks, democratic development across the continent remains a work in progress.

"We are far from getting to the best level," he said. "It is a democracy still struggling to find its way."

DW correspondent Moki Edwin Kindzeka contributed reporting.

articles.title: University of Michigan faculty vote in support of pro-Palestine students facing charges
articles.summary: University of Michigan faculty vote in support of pro-Palestine students facing charges Nearly 60 percent of voting faculty members at the University of Michigan have backed a resolution in support of a dozen former students and staff who are now facing federal criminal charges for their participation in the 2024 anti-war encampments for Gaza. On 12 November, after 2,425 members of the Faculty Senate voted on a motion stating that the Department of Justice's indictment "is part of a broader attack on both Palestine solidarity and labor unions in the United States", results showed 58.2% expressed support. articles.title: A Gaza anche l’ambiente è sotto attacco
articles.summary: Più del 99 per cento di Gaza è contaminato da residui tossici, che avvelenano l’acqua, il terreno e l’aria
articles.preview: Mentre gli abitanti della Striscia di Gaza fanno i conti con il freddo e la pioggia, un altro pericolo incombe su di loro per i prossimi decenni. Metalli pesanti, residui di esplosivi, amianto proveniente dagli edifici distrutti, diossine e contaminanti biologici hanno trasformato il territorio in una “landa desolata e tossica”. Lo denuncia un rapporto pubblicato il 23 novembre dall’ong britannica Oxfam insieme al Conflict and environment observatory, che documenta le conseguenze ambientali e umanitarie dei conflitti armati e delle attività militari.
articles.body:
Mentre gli abitanti della Striscia di Gaza fanno i conti con il freddo e la pioggia, un altro pericolo incombe su di loro per i prossimi decenni. Metalli pesanti, residui di esplosivi, amianto proveniente dagli edifici distrutti, diossine e contaminanti biologici hanno trasformato il territorio in una “landa desolata e tossica”.

Lo denuncia un rapporto pubblicato il 23 novembre dall’ong britannica Oxfam insieme al Conflict and environment observatory, che documenta le conseguenze ambientali e umanitarie dei conflitti armati e delle attività militari.

Usando immagini satellitari, rilevamenti a distanza, analisi spaziali e altri dati open source, la ricerca ha concluso che più del 99 per cento della Striscia di Gaza presenta segni di contaminazione ambientale causata dagli attacchi israeliani degli ultimi tre anni. I residui tossici avvelenano l’acqua, contaminano il suolo e inquinano l’aria, mettendo ulteriormente a rischio le vite dei palestinesi.

Il direttore esecutivo di Oxfam international, Amitabh Behar, spiega nella presentazione del rapporto: “Il genocidio che Israele sta commettendo a Gaza comprende attacchi militari contro l’ambiente, che costituiscono crimini di guerra ambientali e minacciano la vita ora e per generazioni a venire”.

Con tutti e sei gli impianti di trattamento delle acque reflue fuori servizio, ogni giorno 40mila metri cubi di scarichi non trattati finiscono nelle falde acquifere e nel mar Mediterraneo. Le tempeste delle ultime settimanehanno aggravato la situazione perché la pioggia si è mischiata alle acque reflue riversandosi nelle strade e allagando le tende degli sfollati.

Queste acque contaminate poi penetrano nel sottosuolo, rendendo l’esposizione ai residui tossici continua e inevitabile. L’autrice del rapporto Lama Abdul Samad, esperta di questioni legate all’acqua e ai servizi igienico-sanitari, ha detto alla Bbc che a Gaza rischiano di aumentare le malattie respiratorie, i tumori, i danni agli organi, le malformazioni congenite e i casi di bambini nati morti.

L’anno scorso il Programma delle Nazioni Unite per l’ambiente ha calcolato che le operazioni militari israeliane hanno generato più di 61 milioni di tonnellate di detriti in tutta la Striscia di Gaza, il 15 per cento delle quali è potenzialmente a rischio elevato di contaminazione da sostanze pericolose.

Secondo Abdul Samad gestire i danni ambientali nel territorio sarà “estremamente impegnativo, perché la contaminazione è diffusa” e gli ordigni inesplosi impediscono “l’accesso alla maggior parte delle aree”.

Oxfam stima che per rimuovere queste montagne di macerie servirebbero 2,1 milioni di carichi di autocarri con cassone ribaltabile, pari a 736 giri intorno alla circonferenza del pianeta. La quantità di macerie da rimuovere è circa otto volte superiore a quella provocata dal conflitto del 2017 a Mosul, in Iraq.

Il precedente legale sul genocidio

Il rapporto di Oxfam sottolinea che la distruzione ambientale documentata a Gaza potrebbe rientrare nell’ambito di applicazione di diverse disposizioni dello statuto di Roma, che ha istituito la Corte penale internazionale, e della convenzione del 1948 per la prevenzione e la repressione del crimine di genocidio.

La distruzione ambientale non è di per sé un reato punibile in base allo statuto di Roma, chiarisce il rapporto. Tuttavia, prosegue, “la distruzione ambientale mirata o su larga scala può costituire, agevolare o fornire prove schiaccianti di crimini di guerra, crimini contro l’umanità e genocidio, qualora privi i civili delle condizioni necessarie alla sopravvivenza, causi gravi danni o sia usata nell’ambito di un attacco più ampio contro una popolazione civile”.

Sono tutti elementi che potrebbero avere un peso nella decisione della Corte internazionale di giustizia (Cig, il principale organo giudiziario delle Nazioni Unite) chiamata dal Sudafrica a stabilire se Israele sta commettendo un genocidio a Gaza.

L’argomento è tornato nel dibattito internazionale dopo che il 19 novembre la Cig ha emesso quella che Amnesty international ha definito una “sentenza storica” stabilendo che la Birmania (rinominata Myanmar dalla giunta militare) ha commesso un genocidio ai danni della minoranza musulmana dei rohingya durante le operazioni condotte dall’esercito nel 2016 e nel 2017.

Molti esperti sottolineano che la sentenza della Cig rafforzerà la causa per genocidio contro Israele, fissando un precedente secondo cui l’intento genocida può coesistere con un obiettivo militare.

Come scrive Anthony Samrani, condirettore di L’Orient-Le Jour, “il fatto che la Corte internazionale di giustizia abbia accertato il genocidio nel caso birmano non significa necessariamente che farà altrettanto nel procedimento che riguarda Israele. Ma se avesse escluso il genocidio nel caso birmano, sarebbe stato difficile giungere a una conclusione diversa per Gaza. E le ragioni per cui l’ha riconosciuto indeboliscono molto la linea difensiva israeliana”.

Questo testo è tratto dalla newsletter Mediorientale.

articles.title: 'Proof it happened': Photographers reflect on Duterte's drug war
articles.summary: Philippine ex-president Rodrigo Duterte goes on trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Nov 30 for the "crime against humanity of murder", over killings that took place between 2011 and 2019.
articles.preview: Philippine ex-president Rodrigo Duterte goes on trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Nov 30 for the "crime against humanity of murder", over killings that took place between 2011 and 2019. MANILA: Noel Celis's pulse still races whenever a motorcyclist pulls up alongside him at a red light, a legacy of countless nights photographing Philippine ex-president Rodrigo Duterte's bloody drug war.
articles.body:
Philippine ex-president Rodrigo Duterte goes on trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Nov 30 for the "crime against humanity of murder", over killings that took place between 2011 and 2019.

MANILA: Noel Celis's pulse still races whenever a motorcyclist pulls up alongside him at a red light, a legacy of countless nights photographing Philippine ex-president Rodrigo Duterte's bloody drug war.

"They call it riding in tandem," the freelance photographer told AFP of the two-man teams that once roamed the capital, Manila, dealing out death, conceding it remained "scary" after years of death threats tied to his work.

Duterte goes on trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Nov 30 for the "crime against humanity of murder", over killings that took place between 2011 and 2019.

For photographers like Celis, it is as if that period happened yesterday.

The 43-year-old, who worked for AFP at the time, photographed about 200 drug war killings.

One picture showed a young woman cradling the bloody body of her boyfriend shortly after he was gunned down at a busy intersection.

To the mainly Catholic nation, it bore a disturbing resemblance to Michelangelo's La Pieta, a sculpture of the Virgin Mary cradling Christ after his crucifixion. It swiftly became the defining image of the crackdown.

Those working the drug war beat took to calling themselves "nightcrawlers", after a Hollywood film about Los Angeles camera crews chasing late-night mayhem.

MENTAL MAP OF DEATH

At first, the journalists said, the police had no qualms about tipping them off about the killings.

But they clammed up as the public outcry grew, and the photographers resorted to chasing after mortuary vans summoned by police to collect the dead.

It all came flooding back for Dondi Tawatao, 46, when he returned with AFP to a garbage-strewn street where, on a rainy night 10 years ago, he took pictures of two bodies beneath the exposed roots of a banyan tree.

Near them were two handguns he believed were planted there.

"It was very dark, very sinister. It's supposed to be the tree of life, but on that night, it became the tree of death," he told AFP.

After shooting the drug war for four years, the killings became "normalised" to the point where he stopped visiting crime scenes unless they involved at least three corpses.

The long nights rearranged how he saw Manila, he said.

"You sort of have a mental map of where the killings took place. Like randomly, you would be walking, then you realise, 'this was where so-and-so was killed'."

He later left the profession, "primarily to take a rest mentally".

"WE WANT TO APOLOGISE"

Freelancer Kimberly dela Cruz, 36, found her first victim on Manila's rail tracks, and another atop a major bridge.

"It was a full moon, and I thought, 'What a beautiful evening it would have been - except somebody died'," she told AFP of the first.

The head of the man at the second scene was wrapped in packaging tape. He lay next to a cardboard poster that read: "I'm a drug pusher, don't emulate me."

Some of her colleagues would require professional counselling. One suffered from recurring nightmares about the drug war dead coming back to life.

Celis's memories centre on the heart-wrenching keening of victims' wives and mothers, and the sharp, metallic smell of blood.

Residents of the mainly slum-area killing grounds could fear journalists as much as they did police, dela Cruz said.

"I was an outsider. They thought I was an (intelligence operative), police, or somebody that would bring evil," she said.

Celis said photographers wrestled with feelings of guilt over not being able to help, and accusations of "profiting from the suffering of other people".

When he and a colleague attended the wake of the La Pieta victim, they half-dreaded a lynching by angry relatives.

"We went there to apologise for not being able to help," he said, telling the victim's girlfriend the pictures could be evidence were charges ever brought.

"I WAS SHOCKED"

"A picture is powerful," Celis said, "especially at this time, when standing history on its head is in vogue".

Alluding to Holocaust deniers, Tawatao said the photos provided "incontrovertible proof that it happened".

None of the photographers interviewed by AFP believed the drug war solved the country's narcotics problem.

They remain convinced the police murdered thousands to enforce Duterte's will.

But for all, Duterte's arrest and handover to the ICC last year seemed an impossibility - until it happened.

"I was shocked, because I didn't think it was possible. We've only seen the powers that be get away with it," Tawatao said.

Dela Cruz described a "huge sense of relief when (Duterte) was flown to The Hague. It meant some sort of justice was achieved by the families".

"He ordered a war on drugs that killed many people," Celis said.

"It's the natural consequence of his actions."

articles.title: At least 13 Niger soldiers killed in Sanam armed attack
articles.summary: It remains unclear who carried out the attack on Niger's National Guard in Tillaberi, near the Mali border.
articles.preview: It remains unclear who carried out the attack on Niger’s National Guard in Tillaberi, near the Mali border. At least 13 members of Niger’s National Guard have been killed and 20 wounded in an attack on their compound in Sanam, in the west of the country, the Defence Ministry has said. In a statement read on state television, the ministry said the attack on Thursday was carried out by “numerous heavily armed assailants”, referring to the incident as a “terrorist attack”.
articles.body:
It remains unclear who carried out the attack on Niger’s National Guard in Tillaberi, near the Mali border.

At least 13 members of Niger’s National Guard have been killed and 20 wounded in an attack on their compound in Sanam, in the west of the country, the Defence Ministry has said.

In a statement read on state television, the ministry said the attack on Thursday was carried out by “numerous heavily armed assailants”, referring to the incident as a “terrorist attack”.

The ministry gave a provisional toll and said soldiers killed several attackers and destroyed their logistical infrastructure. Operations to track down the attackers are ongoing, it added.

The assault took place at about 5am local time (04:00 GMT), local and security sources told the Nigerien outlet ActuNiger.

Sanam is in the Tillaberi region, near the Mali border, where armed groups regularly attack security forces.

It was not clear who was behind the attack.

The attack comes two days after the ministry said 11 soldiers were killed in an attack attributed to Boko Haram in the Diffa region, in the southeast.

Violence across the border

In neighbouring Nigeria, suspected members of an armed group killed at least 30 people in villages in the central state of Niger on Tuesday.

They described it as retaliation for the killing of many Fulani herders days earlier.

In Nigeria’s northeast, President Bola Tinubu promised on Wednesday to restore peace to a region hit by a rebellion led by Boko Haram and the ISIL (ISIS) affiliate in West Africa Province, as he campaigns for re-election.

articles.title: Trump downplays Russia, China support for Iran during talks with US troops
articles.summary: Trump praises US troops for their role in the war on Iran and says he has spoken to Netanyahu in recent days.
articles.preview: Trump praises US troops for their role in the war on Iran and says he has spoken to Netanyahu in recent days. United States President Donald Trump has claimed Iran possesses missiles capable of reaching Europe and downplayed Russia and China’s support for Tehran while speaking to US military personnel by phone for the Thanksgiving holiday. Taking questions from reporters at his Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida on Thursday, Trump said without “peace in the Middle East”, Iran could launch nuclear attacks against Israel and other countries in the region.

Trump praises US troops for their role in the war on Iran and says he has spoken to Netanyahu in recent days.

United States President Donald Trump has claimed Iran possesses missiles capable of reaching Europe and downplayed Russia and China’s support for Tehran while speaking to US military personnel by phone for the Thanksgiving holiday.

Taking questions from reporters at his Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida on Thursday, Trump said without “peace in the Middle East”, Iran could launch nuclear attacks against Israel and other countries in the region.

“We don’t need Middle East oil. But what we do need is we need peace in the Middle East,” Trump said, as OPEC ministers are scheduled to meet on Sunday to weigh 2027 oil production targets.

The US president and First Lady Melania Trump called US service members deployed across the region to praise their role in the war on Iran, including personnel at the al-Dhafra airbase in the United Arab Emirates and the Prince Sultan airbase in Saudi Arabia.

“Each of you is playing an essential role to protect not only our country today but future generations of Americans by ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon,” he said.

When asked if the US would renew strikes on Iran, the president said: “If we do something, we will definitely hit Pickaxe Mountain.” Trump also told reporters he spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in recent days.

The US is still offering Iran an opening to negotiate, according to Trump, who said: “We’re trying to be nice. We’re giving them every chance to make a deal and save a lot of lives, but I’m not sure if they are gonna take advantage of that.”

He downplayed the importance of intelligence-sharing by Russia and China with Iran, amid reports that the two countries helped Tehran target US bases.

“My meeting with President Xi was an incredible meeting. I think that they’re very little involved with Iran. They could get involved, but involvement to me would mean shooting, not giving them little information,” Trump said during the short news conference.

“We do the same thing, by the way. And you know, when they say that they may be spying on us, well, we spy on them too,” he added.

Trump’s statements come as Iran steps up attacks on US military targets across the region. On Saturday, Bahrain reported an Iranian attack on a civilian industrial facility while Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed it targeted US air defence radars in the country.

Kuwait said on Thursday that an Iranian drone attack on a “vital site” killed two Italian workers and injured four others. Tehran has denied involvement in the attack.

Trump told deployed service members, “You’re going to continue that deployment, and we have victory at hand,” referring to the war on Iran.

“It’s [victory] going to be whenever I want it to be, to be honest,” he added.

articles.title: Yemen war: How do the rival alliances and armed factions stack up?
articles.summary: Yemen war: How do the rival alliances and armed factions stack up? Yemen, where civil war broke out in 2014, has recently been rocked by the worst fighting in years. A truce agreed in 2022 between the Ansar Allah, better known as the Houthis, who control the north, and forces loyal to the government in the south disintegrated when Saudi Arabia bombed Sanaa airport in July. In August and September, the Houthis mounted a quick offensive, recapturing much of the western coast, including the port of Mocha, putting it within close range of ships passing the strategically important Bab el-Mandab strait. The Houthis are now targeting Aden, Yemen’s second city and seat of its internationally recognised government since the group took the capital Sanaa 12 years ago. Meanwhile, the Houthis have tightened their decade-long siege of Taiz, blocking the road to Aden and raising the prospect of its capture. The Saudi-backed pro-government military coalition contains a variety of armed units and local militias, each with different goals, rival leaders and origins, leading to infighting and disorganisation. Allegiances frequently shift and evolve: the Giants Brigade and the National Resistance Forces were each previously backed by the UAE. The leaders of both, like much of the coalition, are now bankrolled by Riyadh amid its fallout with Abu Dhabi. articles.title: Zelenskyy warns of major Russian attack as Trump urges Putin to ‘pull back’
articles.summary: Trump says he urged Putin to 'pull back' military aggression in Europe amid escalating Russian and Ukrainian attacks.
articles.preview: Trump says he urged Putin to ‘pull back’ military aggression in Europe amid escalating Russian and Ukrainian attacks. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine has information that Russia is preparing a new mass strike on the country in the coming days. “Unfortunately, we have information about a new mass strike being prepared by the Russians,” he said in his nightly video address on Thursday. “In the coming days, please pay attention to the alarms of missile threats.” It was the second such warning from Zelenskyy this week.
articles.body:
Trump says he urged Putin to ‘pull back’ military aggression in Europe amid escalating Russian and Ukrainian attacks.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine has information that Russia is preparing a new mass strike on the country in the coming days.

“Unfortunately, we have information about a new mass strike being prepared by the Russians,” he said in his nightly video address on Thursday. “In the coming days, please pay attention to the alarms of missile threats.”

It was the second such warning from Zelenskyy this week. He also had a message for Moscow: “We will rebuild what is ours and retaliate against every Russian strike.”

Trump urges Putin to pull back

US President Donald Trump said he had pressed Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease Russia’s military actions in Europe.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said he spent “a lot of time” in talks with Putin in China on the issue of Putin pulling back “all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe”.

“Thousands of people are being killed each and every month, A COMPLETE BLOODBATH,” Trump wrote. He said he hoped that would allow a deal between Russia and Ukraine to be “made quickly”, which he called “a strong possibility”.

Trump said he updated NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte on the talks during a meeting at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida on Wednesday night.

Latest attacks

Russia struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles overnight, wounding seven people and hitting a shopping centre and two other buildings, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.

Moscow said it hit drone-related sites in the city. Russian forces have attacked Kyiv and other cities almost continuously since September.

Ukraine said its drones hit an oil refinery in Russia’s southern Krasnodar region, oil reservoirs at a Transneft facility in Bashkortostan and the Marinovka military airfield in the Volgograd region.

Ukraine has also widened its attacks at sea. On Monday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine used seven naval drones to hit the Russian corvette Merkury and the cargo ship Angara off Libya. Libyan officials told the Associated Press news agency that the Merkury was heavily damaged but not sunk.

At about the same time, a suspected Ukrainian drone struck the Russia-bound cargo ship Sparta II in the Baltic Sea, near Finland. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the attacks a “very dangerous trend“.

At least four Russian vessels have been targeted this month.

Europe’s funding for Ukraine

European Union leaders are struggling at a summit in Brussels to agree on a new 45 billion euro ($49bn) loan to help Ukraine meet its economic and military needs next year. It would come on top of a 90 billion euro ($99bn) loan, agreed nearly a year ago, that covers most of Ukraine’s government needs for 2026 and 2027.

Early on Friday in Brussels, European Council President Antonio Costa said that 24 member states supported the new loan, as talks on the bloc’s next seven-year budget stretched on.

The loan is tangled up with the EU’s budget for 2028 to 2034, which includes about $110bn for Ukraine over seven years. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has threatened to hold up the budget unless all member states make a “collective commitment” to Ukraine.

North Korea ‘pauses’ arms deliveries

Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (GUR) said on Thursday that North Korea has temporarily halted some military cooperation with Russia after diplomatic tensions between the allies.

It said this includes deliveries of KN-23 ballistic missiles and artillery shells, and Russian military flights over North Korean territory.

GUR said North Korea’s Foreign Minister Choe Son-hui announced the pause last month in response to a Russian deputy foreign minister’s assertion that Moscow would help ease tensions between Seoul and Pyongyang.

GUR also said Pyongyang is holding off on a Russian request to raise North Korea’s military presence in Russia from about 8,500 to 50,000 troops.

It added that North Korean units remain in Russia’s Kursk region and that a North Korean missile unit has been in the Voronezh region since mid-summer, from where Russia strikes Ukraine.

South Korean and Western intelligence agencies have said Pyongyang sent more than 10,000 soldiers to Russia’s Kursk region in 2024, along with artillery shells, missiles and long-range rocket systems.

Strikes continue

On November 20, Russia fired more than 400 drones and 110 missiles at Ukraine, killing eight people, Zelenskyy said.

It was one of the largest attacks of the war and followed Putin’s vow to retaliate for Ukrainian strikes on the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to Crimea.
